# A Call to Action: Bootstrapping an AI-Native Ecosystem {#sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem}

![](images/ch12-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="One team can improve records and comparisons now, while cross-team, physical or silicon, and public-program claims require different shared infrastructure."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The more designers involved in using the new methods, and the better they are able to communicate with each other, the faster the process of cultural integration runs."
>
> — Lynn Conway, *The MPC Adventures* (1981) [@Conway1981MPCAdventures]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Lynn Conway, who with Carver Mead transformed semiconductor design through very-large-scale integration (VLSI) abstractions, documented how shared design rules and networked fabrication turned a new methodology into a community practice. Building Architecture 2.0 presents the same imperative. Decoupling closed-loop design search from proprietary computer-aided design (CAD) lock-in requires open data schemas, neutral consortium benchmarks, and shared infrastructure.
:::

Some of the limits a design team reaches are its own to remove, and some are not. A team that wants to compare two candidates fairly can record what each run cost, keep the runs that failed, and hold the baseline to the same budget, all without asking anyone. A team that wants its comparison to mean something to a second team needs record semantics both teams share. A team that wants a physical claim needs a process design kit it is allowed to use and a shuttle that will carry the die. A team that wants a public benchmark result needs rules it did not write and an auditor it does not employ. The first kind of limit is an effort problem. The other three are coordination problems, and no amount of effort inside one organization removes them. This chapter separates the two, because the separation decides what a team should start tomorrow and what it must wait for others to build.

In the late 1970s, custom integrated circuit design was locked inside vertically integrated semiconductor firms. Carver Mead and Lynn Conway transformed that guild structure into an open academic and industrial discipline. The structured very-large-scale integration (VLSI) abstractions mattered, but so did the multi-project chip methodology and the ARPANET-enabled MPC79 fabrication run that put those abstractions in students' hands [@MeadConway1980VLSI; @Conway1981MPCAdventures]. That precompetitive substrate democratized hardware design, giving rise to the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) MOSIS shared wafer shuttle and launching the fabless semiconductor industry [@MOSIS1981VLSI]. Scaling Architecture 2.0 demands a modern counterpart, and it requires coordinated action across toolmakers, foundries, standards bodies, and universities. In advanced process nodes (3\ nm and below), where full production reticle mask sets reach $\$120\ \text{million}$ (@sec-what-architect-owns) and a single unmodeled timing glitch or power-grid resonance destroys a tapeout schedule, no team can shoulder the empirical learning curve in isolation. @sec-what-architect-owns asked what a single enterprise owns. This chapter asks what the community must build so that any team can record a result another team can trust.

The proposals that follow are grouped by the claim they unblock, and each is traced to the chapter where this book's own argument reached the limit it addresses. Where no chapter reached that limit, the table says so.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
This chapter establishes the following learning objectives:

- **Distinguish** practices a team can adopt locally from shared infrastructure that depends on cross-organizational coordination.
- **Formulate** Open Agentic Interface (OAI) data schemas and signed lineage headers (SLSA attestations, Protocol Buffers, and JSON-LD) for tool interfaces that interoperate across organizations.
- **Match** a physical claim to the implementation path that supports it, separating manufacturable open processes and telemetry-multiplexed shuttles (Tiny Tapeout) from predictive research nodes (ASAP7) and commercial signoff.
- **Structure** neutral consortium benchmark governance (closed/open divisions and total workflow cost accounting) and indexed public repositories of failed runs.
- **Connect** the book's design principles (@sec-appendix-c-design-principles) to what a curriculum must teach and to what a workflow badge can and cannot certify.
:::

## Ecosystem Workstreams and Dependencies {#sec-staging-sequence}

Deploying closed-loop search into hardware design without shared infrastructure risks compounding system fragmentation rather than accelerating progress. The natural commercial instinct in electronic design automation (EDA) is to construct proprietary tool wrappers and hoard private benchmark results. In AI-native design systems, that instinct breeds fragile heuristics that fail outside their training sandbox. When an automated placer or prompt-driven generator trains exclusively on proprietary netlists, its learned representations bake in the unspoken quirks of a specific commercial tool version, standard-cell library, and proprietary process deck. The moment that model confronts an unfamiliar technology target or cross-layer constraint, its predictive confidence collapses. A Layer 2 optimizer can live inside one vendor's flow indefinitely; a Layer 3 system that must carry a design across tools and organizations cannot (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration).

The remedy is not a sequential rollout that waits for consensus. Six proposals follow, and for each one the table separates what a team can start inside its own repositories from what it must wait for others to build, and names the chapter where this book's own argument hit the limit the proposal addresses (@tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence).

| **Proposal** | **Ecosystem action** | **Local starting point** | **Coordination dependency** | **Limit hit (chapter)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Shared data schemas and tool contracts | Retain decision context, artifact identities, commands, returns, failures, and costs in a versioned record. | Cross-team comparison needs common semantics for identities, status, units, and tool results. | Wrappers and learned models that failed to transfer across tool flows (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). |
| 2 | Open implementation paths and cloud silicon shuttles | Exercise an open flow at a named manufacturable or predictive node and state the resulting evidence boundary. | Silicon claims need a manufacturable process design kit (PDK) and shuttle; commercial-node signoff needs foundry-qualified decks, libraries, tools, and access. | Physical timing, power-delivery, and thermal checks left unmeasured (@sec-what-architect-owns). |
| 3 | Consortium governance and matched benchmarks | Run a matched local comparison with pinned tasks, checks, budgets, and total-cost accounting. | A public leaderboard needs neutral rules, shared task versions, audit capacity, and comparator governance. | Benchmark health and matched-baseline failures (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). |
| 4 | Grand challenges and architecture contests | Run a narrow evaluator-owned challenge with a credible baseline and explicit untested conditions. | Cross-organization contests depend on stable interfaces, comparable checks, and enforceable resource accounting. | None in this book. |
| 5 | Public repositories of failed attempts | Retain failed, invalid, timed-out, and rejected attempts alongside successful runs. | Shared repositories need schemas, privacy and licensing rules, stewardship, and controls against misleading or unsafe data. | Censored and purged failed runs (@sec-data-representations-world-models). |
| 6 | University curricula and workforce certification | Teach failure diagnosis, evidence qualification, matched comparison, and authority boundaries now. | A badge also needs published criteria, trained reviewers, appeals, maintenance, and evidence that the badge predicts the claimed practice. | None as a recorded stop; @sec-what-architect-owns names the apprenticeship gap as a risk. |
: **Local adoption can proceed in parallel; shared claims create dependencies.** The proposals identify work that can begin now and the infrastructure required before a team makes broader cross-organizational, silicon, or certification claims. This is a dependency map, not a program that has been run. {#tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence tbl-colwidths="[6,18,25,26,25]"}

Two rows have no entry in the last column. No chapter of this book stopped because it lacked a contest, and none stopped because its engineers lacked a credential; the apprenticeship gap surfaces in @sec-what-architect-owns as a risk to manage, not as a stop the argument recorded. Those two proposals therefore carry less weight than the other four, and the chapter treats them as sketches rather than as infrastructure the argument has earned. The other four each answer a stop the book recorded, and for each the local column names work that needs no permission.

<!-- AUTHOR-THESIS DRAFT 2026-08-31: contract's durable move ("cost one team almost nothing") was asserted, never argued; estimate in words, no numbers -->
What the local column costs a team is worth stating, because the effort argument is otherwise asserted rather than made. Recording the cost of a run means capturing numbers the tools already print, license minutes, wall-clock time, and accelerator hours, into a record the team already keeps; the marginal work is a schema and a habit. Retaining a failed run means not deleting a directory. Running a matched baseline is the one practice with a real price, since the conventional method must run at the same budget as the candidate, and that budget is often the largest line in the study. Even so, the baseline is work a team would have to do anyway to believe its own result. None of these practices needs a second organization to be useful, and each becomes more useful when a second organization adopts it, which is the property that separates the local column from the coordination column.
<!-- END DRAFT -->

Because the coordination dependencies operate concurrently, the proposals group into four workstreams rather than a linear sequence. Open foundations guarantee that software tools and physical fabrication share a common denominator. Governance keeps performance metrics uncorrupted by adversarial tuning or proprietary concealment. Evaluation provides the arenas where AI-native design systems are tested against physical constraints. Skills and review keep the human workforce and the peer-review pipeline able to comprehend and govern the systems the first three workstreams produce. The workstreams exchange records and requirements rather than following one another in order (@fig-ecosystem-roadmap).

![**Ecosystem workstreams share dependencies without imposing a universal adoption order.** Open foundations, governance, evaluation, and skills and review exchange records and requirements. Horizontal connectors show coordination needed for cross-team claims, while local practices within every workstream begin independently. Negative design attempts feed back into schemas, checks, and surrogate calibration.](images/fig-ecosystem-roadmap){#fig-ecosystem-roadmap width="100%" fig-alt="Four coordinating workstreams show open foundations, governance, evaluation, and skills and review. Actions cover schemas, physical-design paths, matched benchmarks, contests, failure repositories, curricula, and review. Dashed connectors indicate shared dependencies rather than a universal adoption sequence, and a feedback arrow returns negative attempts to the foundations."}

The defining mechanism in @fig-ecosystem-roadmap is the feedback loop returning negative design attempts to the shared foundations. Unroutable placements, negative timing slack, and Unified Power Format (UPF) domain violations directly refine schema definitions, benchmark problem suites, property checks, and surrogate calibration. Horizontal connectors represent dependencies for cross-organizational claims, not preconditions for local exploration. Whether this coordination model scales across the semiconductor ecosystem remains an open question.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Anchor AI-Native Design Tools in Open Foundations"}
**The principle:** Scaling Architecture 2.0 across industry and academia requires open data schemas, accessible implementation and reference paths, neutral consortium benchmarks, and qualified repositories of negative design attempts.

**The application:** Begin local cost, provenance, failure-retention, and comparison practices now. Require shared contracts and qualified reference paths before making cross-team comparability, physical, silicon, or certification claims.
:::

## The Precompetitive Open Infrastructure Imperative {#sec-precompetitive-infrastructure}

In deep-submicron and nanoscale fabrication, routing congestion, power-grid IR drop, UPF power-domain isolation, thermal dissipation, and manufacturability demand implementation evidence calibrated to the target node. In advanced commercial nodes (7\ nm, 3\ nm, and 2\ nm), extreme ultraviolet lithography, fin-pitch scaling, gate-all-around nanosheets, and back-end-of-line metal stack RC parasitics mean that physical layout dominates timing closure. Because commercial foundries protect their intellectual property behind strict nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), proprietary signoff tools, and qualified design-rule manuals, academic laboratories and early-stage startups face a structural barrier to physical design exploration.

Expanding open-source physical-design infrastructure and multi-project wafer (MPW) shuttle access narrows this structural divide. Manufacturable open process design kits (PDKs), including SkyWater SKY130 (130\ nm CMOS) [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], IHP SG13G2 (130\ nm BiCMOS with 250\ GHz silicon-germanium (SiGe) heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs)), and GlobalFoundries GF180MCU (180\ nm), support complete open-source physical synthesis, place-and-route, and tapeout fabrication. Coupled with the open-source intermediate representation (IR) infrastructure of Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT)/Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) compiler ecosystem [@CIRCT] and open EDA engines (OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA), these open toolchains render end-to-end design loops fully reproducible without proprietary licensing barriers.

In academic research, ASAP7 serves as a predictive 7\ nm PDK for modeling scaling trends rather than manufacturable signoff [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7].[^fn-predictive-pdk-c12] Because predictive kits simplify complex design-rule manuals and lack calibrated metal-stack parasitics, optical proximity correction decks, and lithography fill-cell models, they cannot substitute for commercial signoff decks when claiming manufacturable power, performance, and area (PPA) closure. A candidate architecture that achieves high ranking under ASAP7 can suffer catastrophic timing inversion or routing collapse when subjected to commercial foundry design rules. Correlating predictive-PDK evaluations with commercial TSMC N7, N3, or N2 characteristics constitutes a distinct research claim requiring matched industrial baselines, explicit parasitic derating models, and documented error bounds.

[^fn-predictive-pdk-c12]: **Predictive process design kit (PDK)**: An open, non-manufacturable cell library and technology model that abstracts geometric and electrical scaling trends for academic research without exposing proprietary foundry design rules or signoff decks [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7].

## Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts {#sec-standardized-data-lineage}

Recording remains an internal hygiene practice decoupled from external disclosure. What a team writes down about its own runs needs no one's agreement; what it exchanges with another team does, and the exchange is where workflow fragmentation across the semiconductor industry begins. In software systems, an untyped JSON payload or loose YAML file is a minor inconvenience. In hardware design, passing untyped strings between a search loop and a physical signoff tool corrupts design state silently. When an optimizer exchanges floating-point spatial coordinates, ambiguous timing slack numbers, or unversioned power-domain declarations through ad hoc scripts, subtle parsing discrepancies propagate without a failing check. A surrogate model might interpret an unconstrained clock port as a zero-delay wire, or an optimizer might infer that an unrouted power rail has zero resistance. Models and tool wrappers developed in one environment then fail completely when transferred to a different CAD flow or technology target (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack).

Just as Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1666 (SystemC) established common modeling semantics across commercial and open environments [@IEEE2011SystemC1666], a standards consortium (such as MLCommons or CHIPS Alliance) could standardize tool and record interfaces before proprietary silos lock in competing APIs. Open schema contracts would let generators, surrogate models, and verification engines interact through stable, machine-readable specifications. The proposed Open Agentic Interface (OAI) would formalize this coordination through three record schemas (@fig-oai-schemas).

- **Design problem formulations.** Explicit declarations of swept parameters, locked constraints, evaluation checks, and acceptance criteria ($s_{\text{design}}$). In the mobile extended-reality (XR) accelerator loop (@sec-architecture-20-ontology), the problem formulation defines search bounds (such as processing element (PE) array sizes from $16 \times 16$ to $64 \times 64$ and static random-access memory (SRAM) capacity 256\ KiB to 2\ MiB), system obligations (3\ W thermal design power (TDP) and 120\ frames per second (FPS) throughput at 4K resolution), target instruction set architectures (ISAs) (RISC-V RV64GCV), interconnects (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe), Compute Express Link (CXL)), and technology targets, distinguishing predictive PDKs such as ASAP7 from commercial TSMC N7 or N3 signoff.
- **Lineage headers.** Declarations of candidate artifacts, parent inputs, transformations, tool flags, structural representations, and environment configurations ($s_{\text{env}}$). A cryptographic hash identifies exact bytes; a Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) attestation binds an issuer to a declaration [@SLSA2026Framework].[^fn-slsa-attestation-c12] Neither mechanism proves semantic correctness, and an attestation remains only as trustworthy as its builder, signing key, and storage path. Lineage headers for SystemC transaction-level model (TLM) memory controllers or high-level synthesis (HLS) kernels (@sec-data-representations-world-models) retain prompt and commit hashes, abstract syntax trees (ASTs), control-data flow graphs (CDFGs), Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) / CIRCT intermediate representation (IR), container digests, seeds, UPF power-domain declarations, and command-line interface (CLI) arguments. To protect proprietary design collateral across organizational boundaries, lineage headers can export structural hashes, compiler pass fingerprints, and bounding-box geometry metrics without disclosing internal transistor topologies, unreleased ISA opcodes, or proprietary foundry cell libraries.
- **Multi-fidelity environmental contracts and tool AI-readiness assessment.** Typed input prerequisites, output schemas, declared error assumptions, status semantics, and property-appropriate checks across analytical models, cycle-level simulators, and register-transfer level (RTL) tools. Assessments verify whether tools such as gem5, Verilator, SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, OpenROAD, Yosys, and OpenSTA expose pinned container interfaces, structured state exports, checkpoint behavior, machine-parsable failures, and documented checks (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking (BMC) reject violations of encoded properties under stated assumptions, but cannot exclude unmodeled deadlocks or behaviors beyond bounded proof depths.

![**The proposed Open Agentic Interface (OAI) would standardize three classes of record.** Design Problem Formulations declare search bounds and obligations; Attempt Lineage Headers identify artifacts and signed transformation declarations; Multi-Fidelity Environmental Contracts declare tool interfaces, assumptions, statuses, and checks. Together they support selective cross-organizational exchange, subject to separate access control, confidentiality, and trust policies.](images/fig-oai-schemas){#fig-oai-schemas width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram of three proposed Open Agentic Interface records: design problem formulation, attempt lineage header, and environmental contract. They capture bounds, artifact identities, transformation declarations, input prerequisites, error assumptions, and tool checks. A bottom box represents selective cross-organizational exchange subject to separate trust and confidentiality controls."}

Serialization is an implementation choice, not the contract. Protocol Buffers give the three record classes typed, versioned message definitions that survive a mixed C++, Python, and Rust toolchain without floating-point parsing drift, and JSON-LD lets a federated repository bind the same execution records to shared ontologies through persistent identifiers without a central database schema. Where CIRCT and MLIR standardize the structural syntax of hardware modules and compiler dialects, OAI would carry the orchestration, lineage, and verification metadata governing how tools and generators manipulate those representations. <!-- AUTHOR-THESIS DRAFT 2026-08-31: EDA reader's first objection is how OAI relates to existing interchange; one sentence, placed beside not replacing --> It would also sit beside the interchange formats the industry already runs on, LEF/DEF for physical geometry, IEEE 1801 UPF for power intent, OpenAccess for design databases, and FIRRTL for generator output, carrying the record of how a run used those artifacts rather than replacing any of them. <!-- END DRAFT --> Each record class withstands a distinct operational boundary: problem formulations survive external parsing, lineage headers survive separation from execution runs, and environmental contracts survive underlying tool updates.

[^fn-slsa-attestation-c12]: **SLSA Attestation**: A machine-readable, cryptographically signed metadata statement that records software supply-chain provenance, build environments, and transformation inputs [@SLSA2026Framework].

## Silicon Shuttles and the Cost Collapse {#sec-silicon-shuttles}

The physical checks that @sec-what-architect-owns left unmeasured, timing at the target corner, power delivery, and thermal behavior, cannot be run on a predictive kit or inside a simulator. They need a die, a die needs a process, and a process needs a shuttle willing to carry a research design. Open physical-design infrastructure extends the precedent of Lynn Conway's MPC79 experiment [@Conway1981MPCAdventures] and the DARPA-funded MOSIS fabrication service [@MOSIS1981VLSI], which aggregated multiple university chip designs onto shared reticle masks over the ARPANET. The economic divergence between commercial manufacturing signoff and university research budgets explains why that infrastructure became indispensable (@fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse).

![**Physical fabrication cost escalation and the open silicon submission renaissance (1981–2026).** (a) Historical full-reticle mask set and commercial MPW prototype costs escalating from $\$35\ \text{thousand}$ ($2\ \mu\text{m}$) to $\$48\ \text{million}$ (3\ nm), breaching academic grant ceilings until open shuttles collapsed entry costs by $3{,}000\times$ [@MOSIS1981VLSI]. (b) Tiny Tapeout submissions and cumulative growth ($152\to 4{,}026$ designs across 22 shuttles) restoring physical silicon verification to university research [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK].](images/fig-shuttle-cost-democratization){#fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse width="100%" fig-alt="Dual-panel plot showing historical silicon fabrication costs and modern open shuttle submission growth. (a) Full mask and commercial MPW prototype costs rising from $35k to $48M from 1981 to 2026 on a log scale, crossing the $50k academic grant ceiling, and dropping below $300 on open PDKs. (b) Tiny Tapeout submissions per shuttle and cumulative growth from 152 to 4,026 verified silicon designs from 2022 to 2026."}

As the historical trajectory demonstrates (@fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse a), the exponential escalation of full-reticle mask sets and commercial MPW rates created an unbridgeable commercial lockout zone for university laboratories between 2007 and 2020. When leading-edge prototype runs crossed $\$100\ \text{thousand}$ to $\$1\ \text{million}$, academic architecture research retreated into software simulation proxies, producing generations of graduate architects who had never brought up physical silicon or debugged a post-fabrication clock-tree defect. The emergence of open PDKs and telemetry-multiplexed shuttle aggregators broke this multi-decade lockout (@fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse b). Platforms like Tiny Tapeout drove a $3{,}000\times$ collapse in fabrication costs, expanding submission throughput from 152 designs on TT01 in 2022 to 4,026 cumulative designs by mid-2026 across three distinct foundries.

Modern open shuttle aggregators (such as Tiny Tapeout, Efabless Open MPW, and Europractice) implement this physical access by providing standardized digital pad rings, automated continuous-integration (CI) hardening frameworks, and shared on-chip scan chains. For AI-generated macros, telemetry-sharing shuttles equip each candidate block with isolated power-monitored rails, ring-oscillator timing characterization across voltage and temperature corners, and JTAG telemetry interfaces. This delivers empirical post-silicon timing, power, and yield measurements back to the community, turning physical fabrication from an inaccessible lottery into an auditable regression environment that calibrates learned surrogates against physical silicon behavior. Containerized open flows improve repeatability, but do not grant commercial-tool rights or close the gap to a different foundry process.

## Consortium Governance and Benchmarking {#sec-neutral-governance}

As open implementation paths lower barriers to physical evidence, evaluation integrity becomes the central challenge. When every research group evaluates its tools on private, cherry-picked RTL blocks with uncounted compute hours and bespoke prompt tuning, published performance margins reflect experimental noise and the optimizer's curse (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization) rather than architectural advances. Multi-stakeholder governance establishes standardized tasks, reference comparators, disclosure rules, and audit protocols, mitigating the benchmark-health failures analyzed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect.

Emulating the governance model of MLCommons and MLPerf [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf], an independent Architecture Automation Working Group under an established body (such as MLCommons, Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation (SPEC), CHIPS Alliance, or IEEE Council on Electronic Design Automation (CEDA)) could establish community-wide evaluation integrity. Separating algorithmic exploration from closed-division compliance while tracking full-system resource budgets is what lets a reported gain be attributed to method rather than to compute scale or uncalibrated tooling. Such a working group would take on three mandates:

- **Reference problem suites.** Problem suites grounded in realistic industrial constraints, spanning 3\ W mobile extended-reality (XR) spatial processing, RISC-V RV64GCV vector clusters, datacenter tensor acceleration, Compute Express Link (CXL) memory expansion, and Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) chiplet interconnect management.
- **Closed and open benchmark divisions.** A Closed Division where entrants compete under locked tool wrappers, fixed compute budgets, and identical baseline matching (evaluating raw algorithmic and search-method efficiency), alongside an Open Division permitting unconstrained search, custom heuristics, or proprietary surrogates provided authors disclose multi-dimensional workflow costs and artifact lineage (evaluating absolute architectural capability).
- **Total workflow-cost accounting.** Mandatory accounting for the multi-dimensional resource vector ($C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$), including graphics processing unit (GPU) compute hours, electronic design automation (EDA) license checkout minutes, and human triage time.

Together the three mandates would give research groups a common baseline. They are also the precondition for any contest, since a challenge without locked divisions and cost accounting rewards compute rather than method.

## Grand Challenges and Design Contests {#sec-grand-challenges}

Where consortium governance would establish neutral baseline rules and cost accounting, competitive grand challenges apply that framework to focus research on unresolved architectural bottlenecks. Standardized traces and open competitions historically propelled innovations in branch prediction through Championship Branch Prediction (CBP) [@CBP2016BranchPrediction], data prefetching through Data Prefetching Championship (DPC) [@DPC2015DataPrefetching], and simulation through ChampSim [@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim], echoing the historical impact of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Grand Challenges in autonomous vehicles [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley] and ImageNet in computer vision [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet]. EDA already runs such contests; the ISPD and ICCAD CAD contests have posed placement, routing, and timing problems on shared benchmarks for two decades, and any Architecture 2.0 challenge would be a track beside them rather than a new institution. No chapter of this book stopped for want of a contest, so what follows is a sketch of three tracks rather than a proposal the argument has earned.

- **Constrained physical PPA generation.** Timing-closed, area-efficient RTL from a high-level specification under a declared power and thermal envelope, judged on physical signoff feasibility without human intervention.
- **Sample-efficient design-space exploration.** Pareto-optimal microarchitectural configurations for heterogeneous workloads under a fixed simulation budget, judged on simulator cycles spent per unit of frontier gained.
- **Adversarial red-teaming and hardware security.** Latent timing exceptions, inserted Trojans, and verification loopholes in generated collateral, judged with SVA and BMC at a declared proof depth.

Whatever a contest crowns, its more durable product is the record of every entry that failed, which is where the next proposal begins.

## Public Repositories of Failed Runs {#sec-open-failed-attempts}

Learned surrogates in hardware design train on corpora that censor their own failures (@sec-data-representations-world-models). When a synthesis or place-and-route job crashes on unroutable congestion, negative slack, or an IR-drop violation, engineering teams typically purge the broken log, so the surviving corpus consists almost exclusively of timing-closed designs and the surrogate trained on it proposes candidates that drive layout engines straight over physical feasibility cliffs the corpus never showed it. Retaining negative results (unroutable floorplans, timing violations, and oscillating power grids) maps the physical shape of failure, bounding exploration spaces and preventing optimizers from rediscovering known unviable topologies. To convert failed runs into reusable community assets, a consortium repository would curate them at three progressive levels.

- **Raw execution traces.** Complete command-line interface (CLI) logs, tool return codes, standard error (stderr) streams, and resource consumption telemetry for failed synthesis and simulation passes.
- **Root-cause taxonomy annotations.** Standardized labels categorizing failures by class: timing violations (worst negative slack $\text{WNS} < 0$), design rule checking (DRC) geometry violations, assertion counterexamples, deadlock states, unroutable congestion maps, and license timeouts.
- **Safe disclosure filters.** Automated sanitization pipelines that convert proprietary physical netlists into normalized graph embeddings, anonymized congestion heatmaps, and relative slack distributions, stripping absolute die coordinates, foundry cell-type names, and top-level block pinouts before external ingestion.

Publishing structured negative data prevents duplicate dead ends across academic and industrial teams and supplies the boundary conditions that calibrate multi-fidelity surrogates. OpenROAD-flow-scripts already publishes a public design set with continuous integration across open PDKs; a failure repository would extend that practice from designs that build to runs that did not. It would also publish the shape of a product's design space, which is why the safe-disclosure level exists and why the licensing question returns among the open questions below.

## Ecosystem Outlook at Scale {#sec-ecosystem-outlook}

The outlook is conditional. If closed-loop exploration reached industry scale on shared foundations, the bottleneck of chip design would move from manual execution toward problem formulation, signoff governance, and cross-layer trade-offs; conventional EDA engines would run headless inside design loops rather than behind per-seat desktop licenses; and the cost of a chip would concentrate in masks, packaging, and physical validation rather than in front-end labor, which favors smaller-volume application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) and the regional laboratories and startups that could not previously afford a custom die. None of that is evidence. It is the outcome the infrastructure above is meant to make possible, and the education and review practices that follow are what would keep the people inside that outcome able to diagnose it.

## Capstone: Curriculum Modernization and Workforce Certification {#sec-curriculum-certification}

Modernizing engineering education is essential to realign the semiconductor workforce with AI-native design methods. Traditional very-large-scale integration (VLSI) curricula prepare students primarily for manual RTL drafting and point-tool execution. In that legacy pedagogical model, students spend months learning idiosyncratic HDL syntax and manual GUI keystrokes for commercial CAD tools. Architecture 2.0 asks for something different. It requires educating architects who formulate requirement domains, construct evaluator-driven verification testbenches, orchestrate multi-tool closed loops, and audit generated designs, across four areas of competence:

- **Specification engineering across requirement domains.** Designing formal specifications and requirement domains across the hardware–software stack.
- **Verification of generated designs.** Developing testbench architectures, property-appropriate checks, and adversarial red-teaming methodologies.
- **Search space formulation.** Defining evaluator-driven search spaces, constraint boundaries, and Pareto trade-off synthesis.
- **Heterogeneous system integration.** Integrating domain-specific accelerators across central processing unit (CPU), neural processing unit (NPU), memory, and packaging boundaries.

As automated tools absorb routine RTL drafting and basic script generation, engineers trained only through prompts and dashboards lose the diagnostic contact that isolates an unroutable floorplan, a dynamic voltage droop, or an intermittent protocol deadlock, and they become the nominal moral crumple zones of @sec-sustaining-responsibility [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones], bearing organizational accountability for automated decisions they cannot inspect. The loss is generational as well as individual. Senior architects acquired that contact by writing Verilog, reading waveforms, and closing timing violations by hand, and the junior engineers who now meet silicon only through a scorecard never acquire it at all. That is the apprenticeship gap @sec-what-architect-owns names as a risk, and its cost falls due later, when a discipline that delegated its routine work finds it has stopped producing engineers qualified to hold commitment authority over the result. Lisanne Bainbridge named the tension four decades ago [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].

::: {.callout-law title="Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation in Hardware Design"}
**The Classical Principle:** Automating routine tasks removes the operator's opportunity to practice fundamental skills, leaving the human least equipped to handle the rare, complex faults that only humans can resolve [@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. The hardware form of the trap is set out in @sec-law-ironies-automation in @sec-appendix-c-laws-paradoxes.
:::

The irony is not resolved by teaching students to prompt better. It is resolved by giving them the diagnostic contact the automation removed, in a setting where a missed fault costs a grade rather than a mask set, and two laboratory practices do that work. In a shadow verification audit, a junior architect follows an automated exploration run as it executes, forms an independent hypothesis about the bottleneck the optimizer is chasing, and audits the generated RTL and its Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) timing declarations before the result reaches senior review, so that the first reviewer of a generated block is the person who most needs to learn to read one. In a fault-injection laboratory, instructors seed a candidate design with a clock-domain crossing (CDC) metastability race, an unhandled finite state machine (FSM) reset state, or a silent false path in its SDC constraints, defect classes @sec-feedback-verification-trust catalogs because RTL simulation cannot see them, and students must localize each with formal tools and waveform slicers. Neither practice adds routine manual work back; both restore the exposure that used to come with it. Students also master open-to-commercial translation layers that map OpenROAD and Yosys telemetry to industrial Synopsys and Cadence signoff flows. A semester course can be built around the four parts of this book, moving from the moonshot and the design loop through data, methods, environments, and feedback to execution, transfer, evaluation, ownership, and the shared infrastructure of this chapter. The design principles collected in @sec-appendix-c-design-principles are its exit test, the moves a student should be able to apply to a problem the course never assigned. The companion site carries the week-by-week version, since a syllabus dates faster than a chapter.

Translating classroom diagnostic practice into peer-reviewed research standards requires institutionalizing computational verification across major academic venues. Conference artifact evaluation committees at venues such as the International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO), Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS), and Design Automation Conference (DAC) could pilot an Autonomous Workflow Certified (AWC) badge grounded in computational reproducibility practice [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science].[^fn-awc-badge-c12] ACM's artifact badging already distinguishes an artifact that is available from one that has been evaluated and one whose results were reproduced; an AWC badge would extend that scheme along the dimensions this book has argued matter for a workflow, from deterministic replay of containerized runs, through signed lineage and total-cost accounting, to surrogate calibration against signoff checks and physical closure on an open manufacturable kit.

The badge names the exact review scope and verification boundaries rather than certifying the final physical architecture or authorizing a commercial silicon tapeout. An AWC badge certifies computational repeatability, lineage provenance, surrogate calibration, and open-flow physical closure of the research artifact; it does not certify commercial foundry signoff, electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection, multi-corner process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) yield qualification, packaging thermo-mechanical qualification, or commercial tapeout liability. Decoupling experimental reproducibility from commercial manufacturing signoff gives reviewers an objective frame in which to audit artifact lineage, check containerized replay, and verify proxy calibration without conflating research reproducibility with commercial signoff.

[^fn-awc-badge-c12]: **Autonomous Workflow Certified (AWC) badge**: A conference artifact evaluation designation attesting to the repeatability and explicit audit scope of an automated design workflow without certifying the physical architecture or authorizing commercial tapeout [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science].

## Open Questions {#sec-ecosystem-open-questions}

The questions that close each chapter of this book state what that chapter's argument rests on and could not settle. The five here are this chapter's residue, and they differ in kind from the ones before them. None can be answered by a single team, because each is about an arrangement between teams, and the infrastructure proposed above depends on the answers.

- **Under what physical constraints do architectural rankings made on open predictive PDKs invert under commercial signoff?** Academic and consortium research relies on open predictive process design kits (such as ASAP7) to evaluate and rank candidate architectures. Predictive kits omit detailed metal-stack parasitics, complex design-rule density limits, and power-grid voltage-droop constraints present in commercial foundry nodes. Until the congestion and scaling thresholds at which predictive rankings flip under commercial signoff are measured, open research rankings remain uncalibrated against foundry silicon, and the measurement itself requires the foundry access the open kits exist to avoid.

- **Who pays for a neutral consortium, and what keeps its rulings neutral once a ruling costs a member money?** MPC79 had DARPA and the ARPANET behind it, and MOSIS ran on federal money for decades. The governance proposed above names no funder, and the parties with the most to gain from shared benchmarks, the tool vendors and foundries, are the ones whose products those benchmarks would rank. MLPerf shows that member-funded governance holds while every member ships a result; what is unknown is whether it holds when a ruling disqualifies one. Whether such a body needs a public funder, a membership structure in which no member's own tool is a benchmarked object, or audit rotated among members' competitors has not been tested.

- **How much of a product's design space does a corpus of its failed runs reveal?** The safe-disclosure level above strips coordinates, cell names, and pinouts, and treats that as sufficient. A failure corpus also records which floorplans a team tried and abandoned, at what congestion and under what slack, and a set of near-misses outlines the design that shipped more precisely than any single successful run does. Nobody has measured how many anonymized failures it takes to reconstruct an unreleased microarchitecture, or whether contribution pooling across many teams, bounded release under a privacy budget, or delayed release after product launch would hold that risk below what a team would accept.

- **How can consortium benchmark suites rotate workloads without destroying historical progress metrics?** Static hardware benchmark suites are quickly memorized or absorbed into model pretraining corpora. Rotating benchmarks every year prevents contamination but destroys longitudinal comparisons, making it impossible to measure whether the discipline's design systems have actually improved across decades. Community benchmarks may have to accept periodic discontinuities to stay relevant, or private, synthetically parameterized task distributions may preserve historical calibration while resisting memorization; nobody has run either long enough to know.

- **Who audits the auditors, and against what?** A consortium that locks divisions, pins tasks, and certifies total-cost accounting becomes the single point every published claim passes through, and its own reference flows, comparator baselines, and audit scripts are artifacts that can drift, be tuned, or be captured. The book asks every team to publish lineage and failed runs; the auditor would have to meet the same standard for its own reference results, and nothing in the proposal says who checks that it does. Whether the answer is adversarial re-audit by competing groups, published lineage for every comparator, or periodic independent replication of the auditor's own baselines is a question the discipline has not had to face, because it has never had such an auditor.

## Summary {#sec-ecosystem-coda}

The Conway epigraph that opens this chapter is a claim about communication, not about tools. Designers who share methods integrate a new practice faster than designers who do not, and the six proposals here are all ways of letting teams share what they currently keep. Four of them answer a stop this book recorded: records that would not transfer across flows, physical checks that could not be run, comparisons that could not be trusted, and failed runs that were never kept. The other two, contests and credentials, answer limits the argument did not reach and are offered as sketches. What unites the six is that each has a local half that a team can start without permission and a shared half that it cannot, and the shared half is what no team can build alone.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Parallel local practice, explicit shared dependencies.** Teams can adopt cost accounting, lineage, failure retention, matched comparisons, and diagnostic training now; broader benchmark, silicon, and certification claims depend on coordinated infrastructure.
- **Open data contracts and lineage.** Proposed Open Agentic Interface (OAI) problem formulations, signed lineage headers, and multi-fidelity tool contracts would support interoperable exchange while leaving access control, confidentiality, and trust to separate policy.
- **Evidence-appropriate implementation paths and shuttle cost collapse.** Manufacturable open PDKs (SKY130, SG13G2) and telemetry-multiplexed shuttles (Tiny Tapeout) drive a $3{,}000\times$ cost collapse for silicon studies at actual nodes, predictive PDKs (ASAP7) support bounded scaling research, and commercial signoff remains tied to foundry-qualified infrastructure.
- **Consortium governance and public failure records.** Neutral working groups would enforce matched baseline comparisons, total workflow cost accounting ($C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$), and closed/open divisions, while indexed public repositories of failed runs supply the negative evidence that success-only datasets withhold.
- **Curricula and certification.** Turning AI-native hardware design into a cumulative discipline requires shadow audits and fault-injection laboratories that preserve the diagnostic contact automation removes, and a workflow badge that certifies replay, lineage, and calibration of a research artifact while refusing to certify commercial tapeout.
:::

<!-- AUTHOR-THESIS DRAFT 2026-08-31: reader-facing bookend close the contract requires; the earlier "write down the questions your own problems raise" move, rewritten in voice -->
The questions that close the twelve chapters of this book were never a research agenda, and reading them as one would miss what they are for. Each set names what a chapter's argument rests on and could not settle, which is the same discipline the book asks of a study record before anyone commits to it. The habit is the point. The next design problem a reader takes on will raise questions none of these anticipated, about a workload the book never named, a tool it never ran, a constraint it never priced. Write those down before the first run, hold the result to them afterward, and the book has done its work without its author present.
